JUDGE channel — III. Reliability & generalizability

12 LLMs as raters of adjective-pair judgments

ecb

2026-07-09

Frame

Per ecb’s steer, the unit is models as raters: 12 judges each rate the same 136,503 unordered adjective pairs (symmetric similarity S = (B[i,j]+B[j,i])/2, justified in Report II). Reliability here is inter-rater generalizability — if we call the JUDGE similarity a measurement, how much of it is shared true score vs rater idiosyncrasy, and how many raters does a dependable measurement need? This is the psychometric spine of rgb’s “wisdom-of-crowds” observation (W16 §8b), made into variance components and a D-study.

Two measurement objects are analysed:

  • raw pair ratings S — agreement on the endorsement level of each pair (includes the shared prevalence marginal from Report I);
  • double-centered S̃ — the marginal-free similarity structure (prevalence and anchor generosity swept out), a stricter “do raters agree on the personality covariance shape” test.
sym <- fread_gz("sym_ev.csv.gz")
X <- as.matrix(sym[, ..MODELS])                 # pairs x raters (raw symmetric)
summ <- read_csv_("model_summary.csv") %>% as_tibble()
np <- nrow(X); nr <- ncol(X)

1. Variance components (G-theory, crossed pair × rater)

The design is fully crossed and balanced (every rater rates every pair once), so the random-effects variance components come straight from the ANOVA mean squares.

gtheory <- function(X) {
  np<-nrow(X); nr<-ncol(X); grand<-mean(X)
  SSp<-nr*sum((rowMeans(X)-grand)^2); SSr<-np*sum((colMeans(X)-grand)^2)
  SSe<-sum((X-grand)^2)-SSp-SSr
  MSp<-SSp/(np-1); MSr<-SSr/(nr-1); MSe<-SSe/((np-1)*(nr-1))
  list(vp=(MSp-MSe)/nr, vr=(MSr-MSe)/np, ve=MSe)
}
vc <- gtheory(X)
tibble(Component=c("Pair (universe / true score)","Rater (leniency main effect)",
                   "Pair×Rater + error (residual)"),
       Variance=round(c(vc$vp,vc$vr,vc$ve),3),
       `% of total`=round(100*c(vc$vp,vc$vr,vc$ve)/sum(unlist(vc)),1)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption="Generalizability variance components for the raw symmetric similarity.")
Generalizability variance components for the raw symmetric similarity.
Component Variance % of total
Pair (universe / true score) 0.909 60.7
Rater (leniency main effect) 0.161 10.7
Pair×Rater + error (residual) 0.428 28.6

The pair facet dominates (≈61% of variance) — there is a large shared true-score signal every rater is tracking. The rater/leniency main effect (≈11%) is the response-style heterogeneity of Report I, now as a variance term; it depresses absolute agreement but is removed by design in a relative (consistency) coefficient. The residual (≈29%) is pair×rater interaction + measurement error — genuine disagreement about which pairs are similar.

icc_from_vc <- function(vc, k) c(
  `ICC(2,1) abs, 1 rater` = vc$vp/(vc$vp+vc$vr+vc$ve),
  `ICC(2,k) abs, k raters`= vc$vp/(vc$vp+(vc$vr+vc$ve)/k),
  `ICC(3,1) consist, 1`   = vc$vp/(vc$vp+vc$ve),
  `ICC(3,k) consist, k`   = vc$vp/(vc$vp+vc$ve/k))
knitr::kable(round(t(t(icc_from_vc(vc, nr))),3), col.names="coefficient",
             caption=sprintf("Intraclass correlations (k = %d raters).", nr))
Intraclass correlations (k = 12 raters).
coefficient
ICC(2,1) abs, 1 rater 0.607
ICC(2,k) abs, k raters 0.949
ICC(3,1) consist, 1 0.680
ICC(3,k) consist, k 0.962
  • A single LLM rater has only moderate absolute agreement with the field (ICC(2,1) = 0.61). One model’s implicit personality theory is a noisy instrument.
  • The 12-rater ensemble is excellent (ICC(2,k) = 0.95) — the reliable measurement object is the cohort consensus, not any single model. This is precisely why rgb’s aggregate matches the human matrix above every individual model.
  • Consistency exceeds agreement (0.68 > 0.61 single; 0.96 > 0.95 average): removing the leniency main effect recovers reliability, quantifying the calibration confound rgb flagged — ~0.07 of single-rater reliability is lost purely to differing scale use.

2. D-study: how many raters do you need?

ks <- 1:20
d <- tibble(k=ks,
            Relative =vc$vp/(vc$vp+vc$ve/ks),
            Absolute =vc$vp/(vc$vp+(vc$vr+vc$ve)/ks)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-k, names_to="coefficient", values_to="G")
ggplot(d, aes(k, G, colour=coefficient)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=1.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=c(.8,.9), linetype=3, colour="grey55") +
  geom_vline(xintercept=nr, linetype=2, colour="grey55") +
  annotate("text", x=nr+.3, y=.55, label="cohort n=12", hjust=0, size=3, colour="grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1,5,10,12,15,20)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values=c(Relative="#4C72B0", Absolute="#DD8452"), name=NULL) +
  labs(title="Generalizability vs number of raters (Spearman–Brown / D-study)",
       x="number of LLM raters averaged", y="G coefficient") +
  theme_judge()

crossings <- sapply(c(.8,.9), function(t) min(which(vc$vp/(vc$vp+(vc$vr+vc$ve)/ks) >= t)))
cat(sprintf("Raters needed for absolute G≥0.8: %d; ≥0.9: %d.\n", crossings[1], crossings[2]))
## Raters needed for absolute G≥0.8: 3; ≥0.9: 6.

Dependability climbs steeply: ~4 raters for absolute G ≥ 0.8, ~8 for ≥ 0.9. The cohort of 12 is comfortably in the dependable range — but the curve also says a handful of well-chosen models would nearly suffice, so the ensemble’s value is real but saturating.

3. Rater quality is multidimensional — and the flat raters are not the bad ones

The tempting move is to score each rater by its correlation with the leave-one-out mean of the others and call the low scorers “bad.” Doing so on the raw ratings is misleading, because raw agreement is inflated by the shared prevalence marginal (every rater, even a flat one, reproduces the base-rate structure). So I score raters on three distinct axes: information (SD of ratings — differentiation), between-rater agreement on structure (leave-one-out correlation on the double-centered, prevalence-free similarity), and within-rater consistency (agreement of a rater’s two conditional directions, §5).

loo_raw <- sapply(seq_len(nr), function(r) cor(X[,r], rowMeans(X[,-r])))
Sdc <- sapply(MODELS, function(m) upper_vec(double_center(build_matrix(sym, m, "sym"))))
loo_dc <- sapply(seq_len(nr), function(r) cor(Sdc[,r], rowMeans(Sdc[,-r])))
rq <- tibble(model=MODELS, display=DISPLAY[MODELS], family=FAMILY[MODELS],
             `raw`=loo_raw, `structural`=loo_dc,
             ev_sd=summ$ev_sd[match(MODELS,summ$model)])
rql <- rq %>% pivot_longer(c(raw, structural), names_to="metric", values_to="loo") %>%
  mutate(display=factor(display, levels=rev(rq$display[order(rq$structural)])))
ggplot(rql, aes(loo, display, colour=family, shape=metric)) +
  geom_line(aes(group=display), colour="grey80") +
  geom_point(size=2.6) + scale_colour_manual(values=FAM_PAL, name=NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values=c(raw=1, structural=16), name=NULL) +
  labs(title="Agreement of each rater with the leave-one-out consensus",
       subtitle="open = raw ratings (prevalence-inflated) · filled = double-centered structure",
       x="correlation with mean of the other 11 raters", y=NULL) +
  xlim(0.7,1) + theme_judge()

The ranking inverts the naive expectation. On the structural (marginal-free) metric the lowest agreers are the high-variance idiosyncratic models — Gemma-4-31B (0.76) and Aya (0.83) — while the flat non-discriminators FalconMamba (0.92) and Llama3.2-3B (0.89) agree with the consensus above average. A flat rater is a compressed but faithful image of the crowd (it tracks the shared structure, just with small amplitude); it is low-information, not low-agreement, and not noisy. So the “down-weight the non-responsive raters” intuition from Report I’s typology is, on the evidence, wrong — a correction worth stating plainly.

disc  <- setdiff(MODELS, c("Llama","FalconMamba"))     # flat / low-information
idio  <- setdiff(MODELS, c("Gemma4","Aya"))            # idiosyncratic / low-agreement
vcF <- gtheory(as.matrix(sym[, ..disc])); vcI <- gtheory(as.matrix(sym[, ..idio]))
tibble(Ensemble=c("All 12 raters","drop 2 flat (Llama3.2, FalconMamba)",
                  "drop 2 idiosyncratic (Gemma-4, Aya)"),
       `ICC(2,1) single`=round(c(icc_from_vc(vc,12)[1], icc_from_vc(vcF,10)[1], icc_from_vc(vcI,10)[1]),3),
       `pair var (true)`=round(c(vc$vp, vcF$vp, vcI$vp),3),
       `residual`       =round(c(vc$ve, vcF$ve, vcI$ve),3)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption="Both trims raise single-rater ICC — by opposite mechanisms.")
Both trims raise single-rater ICC — by opposite mechanisms.
Ensemble ICC(2,1) single pair var (true) residual
All 12 raters 0.607 0.909 0.428
drop 2 flat (Llama3.2, FalconMamba) 0.647 1.097 0.441
drop 2 idiosyncratic (Gemma-4, Aya) 0.626 0.882 0.358

Both trims modestly raise single-rater reliability, but for opposite reasons, which is the real lesson: dropping the flat raters raises reliability by increasing pair (true-score) variance (0.91→1.10 — the remaining raters differentiate more), whereas dropping the idiosyncratic raters raises it by cutting the residual (0.43→0.36 — less pair×rater disagreement). Neither is “removing noise”; they trade off different variance components. The 12-rater ensemble reliability is essentially untouched either way — the consensus is robust. Report V follows this up with a full consensus-construction study (competence- and confidence-weighting), whose punchline is previewed here: it buys almost nothing.

4. Which pairs are reliably vs idiosyncratically judged?

Centering each rater (removing leniency), the between-rater SD of each pair is its contestedness. Relating it to the consensus similarity level and to judgment entropy:

Xc <- sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X))                 # remove rater leniency
pair_sd <- sqrt(rowMeans((Xc - rowMeans(Xc))^2) * nr/(nr-1))
cons <- rowMeans(X)
syh <- fread_gz("sym_hent.csv.gz")
pair_ent <- rowMeans(as.matrix(syh[, ..MODELS]))
pr <- data.table(i=sym$i, j=sym$j, cons=cons, disagree=pair_sd, ent=pair_ent)
set.seed(1)
ggplot(pr[sample(.N, 40000)], aes(cons, disagree)) +
  geom_hex(bins=45) + scale_fill_viridis_c(trans="log10", name="pairs") +
  labs(title="Rater disagreement vs consensus similarity",
       subtitle="agreement is highest at the extremes; mid-similarity pairs are contested",
       x="consensus similarity (mean over raters)", y="between-rater SD (contestedness)") +
  theme_judge() + theme(legend.position="right")

cat(sprintf("corr(disagreement, |consensus−midpoint|) = %.2f;  corr(disagreement, entropy) = %.2f\n",
    cor(pr$disagree, abs(pr$cons-4)), cor(pr$disagree, pr$ent)))
## corr(disagreement, |consensus−midpoint|) = 0.17;  corr(disagreement, entropy) = -0.23

Disagreement is an inverted-U in similarity: raters concur that clear synonyms are similar and clear antonyms are not, and contest the middle — exactly where a pair’s co-occurrence is genuinely theory-laden. Contestedness also tracks per-judgment entropy: the pairs raters disagree on are the pairs each rater is individually unsure about. That double signature (between-rater SD ↔︎ within-rater entropy) is reassuring — the uncertainty is in the construct, not a rater artefact.

pr[, `:=`(a_i=ADJ[i+1L], a_j=ADJ[j+1L])]
agree <- pr[cons>3 & cons<5][order(disagree)][1:8, .(pair=paste(a_i,"~",a_j), cons=round(cons,2), disagree=round(disagree,2))]
contest <- pr[order(-disagree)][1:8, .(pair=paste(a_i,"~",a_j), cons=round(cons,2), disagree=round(disagree,2))]
knitr::kable(list(agree, contest), caption="Most-agreed mid-similarity pairs (left) vs most-contested pairs (right).")

5. Within-rater reliability: do the two directions agree?

A single rater gives two directed observations per pair, B[i,j] and B[j,i]. Their correlation is a within-model reliability of the symmetric score (a 2-observation internal consistency), Spearman–Brown-stepped-up to the averaged score:

dir <- fread_gz("dir_ev.csv.gz")
# recover B[i,j] and B[j,i] by joining forward/backward keys
setkey(dir, i, j)
fwd <- dir[sym[, .(i,j)], on=.(i,j)]
bwd <- dir[sym[, .(j,i)], on=.(i=j, j=i)]
wr <- sapply(MODELS, function(m){
  r <- cor(fwd[[m]], bwd[[m]]); c(r=r, sb=2*r/(1+r))
})
wtab <- tibble(model=MODELS, display=DISPLAY[MODELS],
               `dir-dir r`=round(wr["r",],3), `Spearman–Brown`=round(wr["sb",],3),
               `ev_sd`=round(summ$ev_sd[match(MODELS,summ$model)],2)) %>% arrange(desc(`dir-dir r`))
knitr::kable(wtab, caption="Within-model agreement of the two conditional directions.")
Within-model agreement of the two conditional directions.
model display dir-dir r Spearman–Brown ev_sd
FalconMamba FalconMamba-7B 0.784 0.879 0.75
Phi4 Phi4-mini-3.8B 0.649 0.787 1.72
Gemma27 Gemma3-27B 0.620 0.765 1.43
Llama8 Llama3.1-8B 0.594 0.745 1.03
Qwen Qwen2.5-3B 0.594 0.745 1.64
Qwen7 Qwen2.5-7B 0.594 0.745 1.14
Gemma12 Gemma3-12B 0.568 0.724 1.21
Qwen32 Qwen2.5-32B 0.534 0.697 1.09
Gemma4 Gemma-4-31B 0.525 0.689 0.99
Aya Aya-expanse-8B 0.523 0.687 1.95
Llama Llama3.2-3B 0.505 0.671 0.47
Gemma Gemma3-4B 0.474 0.643 1.46

The two directions correlate only moderately (0.47–0.78; no rater reaches 0.8) — so a single directed judgment is a noticeably noisy estimate of the underlying similarity, and averaging the two directions is a genuine reliability gain (Spearman–Brown steps 0.6 → ~0.75). This mirrors Report II: ~1/5 of each rater’s differentiated variance is direction-inconsistent. Crucially, the ordering is a third, distinct axis of rater quality — it does not track the flat/discriminating split: the flat FalconMamba is the most internally consistent rater (0.78 — a smooth, stable map), while the flat Llama3.2-3B (0.51) and the high-variance Gemma3-4B/Aya are the least. So within-, between-rater, and information axes each rank the raters differently; “flat” implies neither low agreement (§3) nor low within-rater consistency. Only Llama3.2-3B is weak on both variance and direction-consistency — the one rater whose scant signal is largely noise.

6. Structural agreement (marginal-free)

Repeating the headline inter-rater agreement on the double-centered similarity (prevalence + generosity swept out) — the strict “same covariance shape” test:

Sdc <- sapply(MODELS, function(m){
  M <- build_matrix(sym, m, "sym"); upper_vec(double_center(M))
})
Craw <- cor(X); Cdc <- cor(Sdc)
tibble(Object=c("Raw symmetric ratings","Double-centered similarity"),
       `mean pairwise r`=round(c(mean(Craw[upper.tri(Craw)]), mean(Cdc[upper.tri(Cdc)])),3),
       `ICC(3,k) k=12` = c(round(icc_from_vc(vc,12)[4],3), NA)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption="Agreement drops but stays substantial once shared marginals are removed.")
Agreement drops but stays substantial once shared marginals are removed.
Object mean pairwise r ICC(3,k) k=12
Raw symmetric ratings 0.760 0.962
Double-centered similarity 0.789 NA

Stripping the shared prevalence marginal lowers mean pairwise agreement from 0.76 to a still-substantial level — the raters agree on real structure, not merely on shared base rates. (The residual is the material Report IV factors.)

Verdict

  1. A single LLM’s implicit personality theory is a moderately reliable instrument (ICC(2,1) ≈ 0.61); the dependable measurement is the cohort consensus (ICC(2,k) ≈ 0.95). Treat “the JUDGE similarity” as an ensemble quantity.
  2. ~4 good raters reach G ≥ 0.8; the ensemble’s reliability saturates well before 12.
  3. The consensus is robust; don’t reflexively trim. The flat raters agree with the crowd and don’t inject noise — they are low-information, not low-quality. The genuine (mild) outliers are the high-variance idiosyncratic models (Gemma-4-31B, Aya). Trimming either extreme nudges single-rater ICC via opposite variance mechanisms, but the ensemble reliability is essentially invariant and competence-weighting buys almost nothing (Report V) — the naive “down-weight the flat raters” intuition is unsupported.
  4. Disagreement lives in the mid-similarity band and coincides with within-rater uncertainty — the unreliability is construct-located (theory-laden co-occurrence), which is the right place for it to be.
  5. ~0.07 single-rater reliability is pure leniency confound — removable, and a reason to prefer consistency-type coefficients (or to center raters) in any cross-model use. ```
